readings.title: The School Lunch Survey
readings.passageEn: A school wanted to know whether students liked the new lunch menu. An early survey asked, “Don't you agree that our delicious new lunches are much better?” Several students said this sounded like a question with a preferred answer. The committee rewrote it: “How satisfied are you with the new lunch menu?” It also offered a range of possible responses. The second version was not perfect, but it reduced the pressure to praise the food. Students compared the responses obtained from both versions of the question. They saw that wording could influence how comfortable someone felt disagreeing with a statement. They also noted that a balanced response scale should allow dissatisfaction as well as praise instead of quietly pushing everyone toward the same answer. Good information depends not only on how many people answer a survey, but also on how clearly and fairly each question is written.

readings.title: The Warm Roof Problem
readings.passageEn: On a summer afternoon, two classrooms in the same school felt very different. One classroom was directly under a dark roof, while the other had shade from tall trees. Students wondered why the first room felt hotter. They measured the temperature at several times and found that the difference was greatest in the early afternoon. The principal used their results to test a light-colored roof coating on a small section of the building. The school did not assume that one measurement proved everything. It continued to collect data during different kinds of weather. The class also discussed whether the two rooms were otherwise similar. The number of students, open windows, and time of day could all influence the readings. The teacher encouraged them to record these conditions rather than assume that roof color explained the entire difference. This made the project a lesson in comparison as well as heat. The project showed how a familiar discomfort can become a scientific question when observations are recorded and explanations are tested.

readings.title: Why the Stream Changed
readings.passageEn: A class visited a stream after several days of heavy rain. The water looked brown, and leaves had gathered near a narrow bridge. One student guessed that a factory upstream had released waste. The teacher reminded the class that the color alone did not identify a cause. Rain could wash soil into the water, and fallen leaves could block the flow. Students recorded their observations and compared them with photographs taken in dry weather. They also checked whether factories were located nearby. A student proposed taking a water sample at the same location after the next period of dry weather. Another suggested checking records of nearby construction activity. The teacher welcomed both ideas because they could produce new evidence rather than simply repeat an early suspicion. The group kept track of which explanations were still uncertain. Their investigation did not immediately produce a final answer, but it helped them distinguish possible explanations from claims supported by evidence.

readings.title: A Small Change in Energy
readings.passageEn: A family wanted to reduce electricity use at home. At first, everyone blamed the refrigerator because it was always running. They placed a small meter on several appliances and compared the results over a week. The measurements showed that one old electric heater used much more energy than expected during cold evenings. The family decided to adjust how long they used it and improve insulation near a window. Their bills did not fall to zero, but the family learned where small changes would matter most. They also considered the cost of replacing equipment and decided to begin with steps that required little money. The meter gave the family a baseline for checking whether the changes worked. It prevented them from giving credit to an improvement that might simply have resulted from warmer weather during the following week. Good decisions about saving energy depend on actual patterns of use, not simply on which appliance looks most noticeable.

readings.title: The Missing Trees
readings.passageEn: A neighborhood planted young trees along a walking path. After a year, some were growing well while others had hardly grown. Residents first assumed that the smaller trees had received less sunlight. A local gardener compared the sites and discovered that several trees stood where water collected after rain. Their roots often remained in very wet soil. The group improved drainage in those spots and continued monitoring the trees. Growth varied for many reasons, but the new observation gave the residents a specific problem to address. The gardener warned that some young trees need different amounts of water even when planted along the same path. Residents therefore recorded the soil conditions and tree species together. Over time, those notes could help them distinguish a drainage problem from differences in the plants themselves, making future choices more informed. The experience reminded them that a solution works better when it responds to the mechanism behind a problem rather than to an attractive first guess.

readings.title: The Two Helpful Opinions
readings.passageEn: A school committee needed to choose between two playground designs. One design offered more open space for ball games, while the other included quiet places to read or talk. Members initially argued that their preferred design was obviously best. Then one student suggested listing the needs of different groups. The committee asked younger pupils, older pupils, and teachers how they used the playground. The responses did not produce a perfect answer, but they revealed a compromise: divide the area into flexible zones. Younger children wanted open areas to run, while students preparing for exams requested places to sit quietly. Teachers were concerned about supervision and safe movement between zones. These different priorities explained why a design that appeared ideal from one viewpoint could create problems for others. The committee had to consider more than the loudest opinion. Comparing viewpoints can improve a decision when it helps people notice needs that their own experience does not show.

readings.title: A Popular Choice
readings.passageEn: A class voted on which book to read together. The most popular title won, but a few students worried that they would not be able to understand it. The teacher asked whether popularity was the only useful criterion. The class discussed difficulty, length, available copies, and the purpose of the project. They finally selected a different book that most students could read while still offering challenging ideas. The experience did not show that voting was useless. It showed that a decision can be democratic and still need careful thought about the standards being used. The teacher asked the class to imagine a different project in which students selected a book only for enjoyment. In that setting, popularity might be a reasonable priority. For a group discussion requiring shared understanding, however, accessibility and the ability to support thoughtful conversation mattered more. The same choice could be judged differently under different goals. A large number of votes does not automatically mean that a choice fits every goal.

readings.title: The Lost Wallet
readings.passageEn: On the way home, Yuna found a wallet near a bus stop. She noticed a name card inside but did not recognize the owner. Her friend suggested posting a photograph of the card online to find the person quickly. Yuna worried that doing so might reveal private information. Instead, she took the wallet to a nearby service desk where lost items were recorded and returned. It took longer than making a public post, but the method protected the owner's information. The situation showed that a quick solution is not always the best one. Her friend initially believed that a public post would probably reach the owner quickly. Yuna agreed that speed mattered but asked who else might see the name and other details in the photograph. The friends discussed how sharing a small piece of information online could have consequences that were difficult to control afterward. A useful choice should consider both its immediate result and its possible consequences for other people.

readings.title: The Strange Average
readings.passageEn: Two classes compared their daily reading time. In Class A, most students read for about twenty minutes. In Class B, several students read for only a few minutes, but one student read for three hours. The average reading time in Class B appeared surprisingly high. A student concluded that everyone in Class B read more than those in Class A. Her teacher explained that an average describes a group but can hide important differences among its members. They examined the individual values and compared the median as well. To make the difference visible, students drew two simple dot plots. One had values clustered close together; the other included a value far from most of the group. The diagrams made it easier to see why a mean can rise when only one observation is unusually large. They also discussed whether the median answered a different question. A single number can be useful, but it should not replace questions about how the underlying data are distributed.

readings.title: The Bicycle Rack Debate
readings.passageEn: A school council proposed adding bicycle racks near the main gate. Supporters argued that secure parking would encourage more students to cycle, reducing traffic around the school. Opponents pointed out that the entrance was already crowded during the morning rush. At first, the council discussed the proposal as a simple choice between building racks and doing nothing. A teacher asked both sides to identify the evidence they needed. Students counted bicycles arriving at different times and mapped how pedestrians crossed the entrance. The council eventually recommended placing racks beside a quieter side gate. The discussion improved when competing arguments were treated as useful information rather than as personal attacks. The data showed that many cyclists arrived just before the first bell, at the same time that pedestrians entered through the main gate. The council debated whether painting separate lanes would be enough or whether a different location would be safer. When the side gate appeared promising, students visited it again to check visibility and crossing distance. The final recommendation was based on several small observations rather than a single dramatic argument. A good decision can grow from disagreement when each side is willing to test its assumptions.

readings.title: A Ban on Plastic Bottles?
readings.passageEn: A youth club considered banning disposable plastic bottles at its events. One member argued that the ban would reduce waste. Another replied that some visitors might forget reusable bottles and have no easy way to drink water. The club could have chosen one argument and ignored the other. Instead, it considered a refill station and a small supply of reusable cups. Members also measured how many bottles were discarded during the next two events. The revised plan was more complicated than a simple ban, but it addressed both environmental aims and visitors' needs. The club also discussed the cost of maintaining the refill station and cleaning reusable cups. One member suggested that signs explaining where to find drinking water might be as important as the ban itself. They planned to check whether the change reduced disposable waste without leaving anyone unable to get water. Evaluating the policy would require observing behavior, not merely announcing a rule. An effective argument does not have to deny every objection. It can become stronger by acknowledging a concern and proposing a practical response.

readings.title: When Numbers Make a Case
readings.passageEn: A town wanted to plant more trees on a busy street. A campaign poster claimed that trees would make the area healthier and more pleasant. Many residents liked the message, but the town council needed a way to decide where planting would help most. Volunteers measured how hot different sidewalks became in the afternoon and recorded which blocks had little shade. They found that some crowded stops were much hotter than nearby shaded streets. These observations did not prove every claimed health benefit. However, they provided a concrete reason to begin in specific locations. The volunteers noticed that a wide sidewalk with few trees was not always the hottest place. Building shade and the direction of the afternoon sun also mattered. This led them to divide the street into smaller sections and compare conditions at similar times. Their report made a limited claim: the measured locations appeared to deserve early attention. It did not promise that planting trees would solve every environmental concern. A persuasive proposal becomes more useful when broad goals are connected to evidence that guides an actual decision.

readings.title: The Robot Homework Claim
readings.passageEn: During a class debate, one student claimed that robots would soon complete every kind of homework. He pointed to an online video in which a machine solved a math problem. Another student asked whether solving one problem proved that the system could understand a complex essay or explain a scientific experiment. The class agreed that the video demonstrated a particular ability, but not the broad claim. They rewrote the original statement: some automated tools can assist with certain homework tasks under specified conditions. The revised claim sounded less dramatic, yet it could be tested. The teacher asked students to separate a claim about what a tool can do today from a prediction about what it might do in ten years. Both questions were interesting, but they required different kinds of evidence. The video supported a description of one task under one set of conditions. It could not settle whether the system would reliably handle unfamiliar situations or provide explanations that a learner could verify. Strong reasoning often requires limiting a statement to what the evidence actually supports instead of making the most exciting possible prediction.

readings.title: A Quiet Hour Proposal
readings.passageEn: Residents of an apartment building disagreed about a proposal for quiet hours in a shared study room. Some wanted complete silence throughout the day. Others said that small group discussions were necessary for learning. Rather than labeling either group unreasonable, the building committee asked when different kinds of activities usually took place. A short survey showed that many students studied alone in the evening, while group projects were more common on weekends. The committee proposed silent hours on weekday evenings and discussion periods on weekend afternoons. Not everyone obtained a perfect schedule, but most people could explain the reasoning behind the new rule. The committee agreed to review the rule after one month instead of assuming that its first proposal would be perfect. Residents could report whether the schedule helped them study and whether the discussion periods were long enough. This feedback mattered because a shared room serves people with changing routines. The committee also considered posting clear signs to avoid disagreements about what was allowed at a given time. Compromise does not mean ignoring conflicting values; it means designing a choice that recognizes them.

readings.title: The Old Photograph
readings.passageEn: A local museum found a photograph labeled “Opening Day, 1960.” The picture showed a line of people outside a building, and a volunteer assumed it recorded the museum's opening ceremony. Another volunteer noticed that the building's sign used a name adopted several years later. The museum checked newspaper records and realized that the photograph came from a special exhibition, not the original opening. The image itself had not changed, but a small piece of background knowledge changed its interpretation. Readers face a similar challenge when a phrase or pronoun seems clear at first glance. The volunteers examined another photograph from the same collection and found that its handwritten date was difficult to read. This reminded them that archive labels can contain mistakes even when the original objects are authentic. They decided to record both their sources and the level of confidence in each identification. Visitors could then see how historians reach conclusions instead of receiving an uncertain interpretation as an unquestionable fact. The first reasonable interpretation should remain open to revision when later information does not fit.

readings.title: This Change Mattered
readings.passageEn: A small town replaced some streetlights with lamps that used less electricity. The new lamps also directed light downward instead of into nearby windows. Residents reported that their rooms were darker at night and that the street still felt safe. This change helped the town address two different concerns: energy use and unwanted light entering homes. In a news report, the phrase “this change” would refer not merely to the purchase of new lamps but to the overall replacement and adjustment of lighting. Understanding such expressions requires readers to connect several nearby facts. The town also received a few complaints that the new lighting seemed unfamiliar. Staff compared the actual visibility at crossing points before deciding whether to adjust individual lamps. They did not want to save energy at the expense of safe movement. The newspaper's description connected these choices into one broader account of design, public feedback, and the different effects of a technical change. Words like this, these, and such often point to ideas rather than to a single visible object.

readings.title: The Book Recommendation
readings.passageEn: A library website began recommending books based on a visitor's borrowing history. A student who often borrowed mysteries received a long list of similar novels. At first, she was pleased because choosing had become easier. After several months, however, she noticed that she rarely saw history, poetry, or science books. The system had learned her past preferences, but it did not know what unfamiliar subjects she might enjoy. She began choosing one book each month from a shelf outside her usual interests. A librarian described the system as a useful starting point rather than a complete guide to the student's future interests. The student discovered that a poetry collection reminded her of themes in a mystery novel. That connection would not have appeared in a list based solely on her previous borrowing. She later asked the librarian for a recommendation that surprised her instead of one that matched her history. The experience suggested that personalization can save time while also narrowing what we encounter if we never explore beyond its suggestions.

readings.title: A Bird's Warning
readings.passageEn: In a wetland, researchers noticed that some birds became unusually quiet before a heavy rainstorm. A visitor concluded that birds could always predict storms. The researchers were more cautious. They explained that birds might respond to changes in wind, pressure, or other conditions, but the observation alone did not show which signal mattered. They compared observations across many days, including calm days when birds also became quiet. The pattern was less simple than the visitor had expected. A clue becomes useful when we ask what else might explain it. The researchers also considered the possibility that the birds were responding to human activity rather than to the weather itself. On some days, fewer visitors walked through the wetland, which might have changed the animals' behavior. The team needed repeated observations to distinguish among these explanations. A single striking event could inspire a hypothesis, but it could not automatically confirm the mechanism behind the pattern. In reading, an implied conclusion should likewise fit the evidence without claiming more certainty than the passage allows.

readings.title: The Locker Near Home
readings.passageEn: A delivery company installed shared parcel lockers beside a subway station. The company expected every resident to prefer collecting packages there instead of waiting at home. Many commuters welcomed the service, especially those who returned late from work. Yet some elderly residents and people carrying heavy items found it difficult to travel to the station. The company revised its plan and kept home delivery available for people who needed it. The change revealed an important distinction between an average benefit and a benefit shared by everyone. A survey showed that convenience had several meanings. For a commuter, collecting a package on the way home saved time. For someone with limited mobility, traveling to a locker created an extra trip. The company had initially counted how many people used the new service without asking which groups had stopped receiving a convenient option. The revised evaluation included both use rates and access for people with different needs. A policy can work well for many users while still creating difficulties for a particular group. Understanding a claim about improvement therefore requires asking who gains, who does not, and under what conditions.

readings.title: A Library Without Walls
readings.passageEn: A city library noticed that teenagers rarely borrowed printed books after school. Instead of assuming that they had lost interest in reading, the librarians asked students what made visiting difficult. Some said the library closed before their clubs ended. Others wanted short articles or audio stories they could access on a bus. The library extended its digital collection and created a small evening reading corner. Borrowing increased, but the librarians did not claim that one format was best for every reader. The new services worked because they focused on access to reading rather than on preserving one traditional way of borrowing. The librarians also kept printed books and spaces for group activities. Some readers enjoyed turning pages and meeting friends at the library, while others preferred listening to a story during a journey. The new collection offered more ways to participate rather than replacing an older format with a new one. Staff evaluated success through actual use and comments about convenience, not just the number of digital titles purchased. The purpose of a library is broader than the building and the paper books inside it.

readings.title: The App That Counted Days
readings.passageEn: An app encouraged users to study by displaying the number of consecutive days they had opened it. At first, a student enjoyed watching the number grow. When she became sick and missed one day, the counter returned to zero. She felt as if all her earlier work had disappeared, even though she had learned many words. The developers changed the display to show total practice days, recently mastered words, and progress over several weeks. The new dashboard still rewarded regular learning, but it did not turn one missed day into a failure. The developers also removed the message that had warned users they were about to lose a streak. Some students had opened the app only to protect their counter, without completing a meaningful exercise. The team began testing whether users could explain the words they had supposedly mastered. That measure was harder to display as a simple badge, but it was closer to the purpose of the product. Better feedback supported learning instead of anxiety about a number. Feedback is useful when it helps people understand and improve their behavior, not when it makes a simple number more important than learning.

readings.title: The Museum of Ordinary Things
readings.passageEn: A neighborhood museum planned an exhibition about daily life fifty years ago. Some volunteers wanted to display only rare and expensive objects. Others suggested including ordinary lunch boxes, school notebooks, and bus tickets. The museum decided to combine both kinds of items. A rare object could attract attention, while a familiar one might help visitors imagine the routines of people who lived in that period. The exhibition used short stories from local residents to explain why simple objects mattered. Visitors began asking questions about how families traveled, worked, and learned. The most valuable historical object is not always the one with the highest price. One visitor recognized a bus ticket that her grandmother had kept for decades. It started a conversation about how commuting patterns changed as the town grew. Another family noticed a school notebook whose exercises looked surprisingly familiar. The museum used these reactions to design questions beside the displays. What did the object tell visitors about time, work, access, or family routines? Small objects became clues to larger processes. Ordinary things can reveal how broad social changes were experienced in everyday life.

readings.title: The Science of a Fair Game
readings.passageEn: A group of students designed a quiz competition in which faster answers earned more points. At the first event, some participants answered quickly but guessed incorrectly, while others took time to reason through difficult questions. The organizers discovered that their scoring system rewarded speed more strongly than understanding. They changed the rules so that correct explanations received additional points, and the difficulty of a question mattered more than a fraction of a second. The new rules did not remove competition. Instead, they aligned the game with its educational purpose. Measures shape behavior because players naturally pay attention to what earns rewards. The organizers also tested whether the new scoring rules were easy to understand. If judging explanations took too long, the competition would lose its energy. They created short rubrics and allowed players to see why points were awarded. Students became more willing to explain their thinking, including when they were uncertain. The adjustment illustrated that a measurement system can influence not only final rankings but also the strategies people choose while learning. When evaluating a system, we should ask whether the score represents what we truly want to improve.

readings.title: The Bridge as a Public Space
readings.passageEn: A city announced a new pedestrian bridge across a river. Engineers considered cost, strength, and the time needed for construction. Community groups added another question: could the bridge become a place where people wanted to spend time, rather than merely a way to cross? Their proposal included small viewing areas, safe bicycle access, and signs explaining the river's history. Some features increased the budget, so the city had to decide which were feasible. The discussion showed that infrastructure is not only a technical object. It shapes how residents move, meet, and experience their surroundings. An early design had placed a large viewing platform in a narrow section of the bridge. Engineers warned that the platform might interfere with pedestrian flow during busy hours. Community representatives suggested moving the area closer to the riverbank. This preserved space for people to stop without making the main crossing less comfortable. The city still needed to weigh construction costs against the social value of the additional features. The central challenge was to balance the bridge's basic transport role with its potential as a shared public space.

readings.title: A Battery Surprise
readings.passageEn: Two students tested small rechargeable batteries in model cars. They assumed that the battery with the highest advertised capacity would always produce the longest drive. During their first trials, however, the cars stopped at different times depending on the speed and the weight they carried. The students checked whether the batteries had started fully charged and repeated the test under the same conditions. The largest battery sometimes performed better, but the result was not as simple as the package labels suggested. The exercise revealed why a comparison must control other factors. The teacher reminded students that advertised capacity is measured under particular conditions, and real devices may use energy at different rates. The group decided to keep the motor and route the same while changing one battery at a time. They recorded temperature and charging time as well. Their later trials were less exciting than the first, but they produced evidence that could be interpreted more confidently. Testing a claim often requires repeating ordinary steps carefully. If the conditions change at the same time as the feature being tested, it becomes difficult to identify which factor caused the difference.

readings.title: The Vertical Garden
readings.passageEn: A school considered growing vegetables on several shelves under artificial lights. A student argued that using more shelves would always produce more food. The science club built two small models and measured the harvest from each. The taller model had more planting space, but some plants received less light because the arrangement blocked it. The club also discovered that higher shelves were harder to water and inspect. Adding layers created both opportunities and new constraints. A better design required balancing space, light, access, and maintenance instead of maximizing only the number of shelves. The students also asked whether a single harvest was enough to judge the designs. Some vegetables grew faster than others, and maintenance time might change over several months. They recorded the hours spent watering and checking each layer so that labor would not disappear from the comparison. A larger crop would be less impressive if it required far more effort than a smaller system. The club began to discuss productivity as the result obtained relative to resources used. The lesson was that improving one part of a system does not guarantee that the entire system will improve by the same amount.

readings.title: A Runner's Pace
readings.passageEn: A student training for a long-distance race tried to run as fast as possible at the beginning of every practice session. She often slowed sharply near the end. Her coach suggested starting at a manageable pace and saving energy for later stages. Over several weeks, she compared her total running times rather than judging only the first kilometer. Her average performance improved even though the first kilometer became slower. The result seemed surprising because going slowly at first looked like giving up speed. In fact, the new strategy reduced the cost of tiring too early. The coach showed that a race has several stages, each affected by the energy spent earlier. The student began using a watch to record how evenly she covered each section. On some days, weather and fatigue still made her times worse, so she looked for a pattern across repeated practices rather than celebrating one unusually fast run. The strategy encouraged planning for the whole distance instead of focusing on a dramatic opening. A good plan sometimes sacrifices a small immediate gain to protect performance over the whole task.

readings.title: The Translation That Missed the Joke
readings.passageEn: A language club compared two translations of a short comic story. The first version replaced each word with its most common dictionary meaning. The second considered the situation, the speaker's intention, and a joke based on an unusual expression. Although the second version was less literal, students found it easier to understand why the characters laughed. The teacher reminded them that translation involves decisions about meaning at several levels. A sentence can be grammatically correct and still fail to convey the intended message. This is especially true when humor, politeness, or cultural assumptions matter. Students discovered that there was no single word in the target language that produced exactly the same double meaning. They suggested several alternatives and discussed what each version preserved or lost. One translation kept the original wording, while another kept the surprising relationship between the characters' statements. The class learned that a translator sometimes chooses among imperfect options according to the purpose and audience of the text. Accurate communication sometimes requires moving beyond a word-for-word match while keeping the central intention of the original.

readings.title: A Shore for Two Species
readings.passageEn: A coastal town planned to improve a walking path beside a wetland. Residents wanted a safer route, but wildlife groups warned that bright lights at night could disturb animals. Engineers first considered keeping the new lights on all evening. A student team suggested using shielded lamps and setting lower brightness during quiet hours. The town tested the design in one area while recording visibility for walkers and signs of animal activity. The trial could not answer every long-term ecological question, but it helped reveal the trade-off between different goals. The trial team invited both evening walkers and local nature observers to report their experiences. Walkers focused on whether they could see the path safely, while observers paid attention to activity near the wetland edge. These reports were not a substitute for longer ecological research, but they could help identify immediate problems. The engineers planned to revise individual lighting settings rather than treat the first design as final. Instead of treating human access and environmental care as mutually exclusive, the town looked for conditions under which both could be improved.

readings.title: A City After Heavy Rain
readings.passageEn: After repeated summer floods, a city considered building a larger drainage tunnel. Some engineers argued that the tunnel would reduce water on major roads. Community groups pointed out that homes in low-lying neighborhoods might still flood if local drains were blocked. The city compared several options: a tunnel, better maintenance of neighborhood drains, and small parks designed to hold rainwater temporarily. No single option solved every problem under every storm scenario. The city therefore evaluated combinations of actions, their costs, and the neighborhoods each would protect. The central challenge was not simply to choose the largest project. Some neighborhoods had experienced flooding even during moderate storms, while others faced trouble only when water rose unusually high. This meant that average rainfall was not enough to judge local risk. The city developed several plausible rainfall scenarios and asked how each investment option would perform. The proposals also differed in construction time: a major tunnel would take years, while drain maintenance could begin sooner. These differences mattered to residents facing near-term danger. It was to build a system that remained useful when future rainfall and local conditions differed from expectations.

readings.title: The Driverless Shuttle
readings.passageEn: A university introduced an autonomous shuttle on a short campus route. The vehicle could follow a planned path and stop at marked stations without a driver holding the wheel. Some observers described the system as completely independent. In practice, staff monitored operations and could intervene when unusual obstacles appeared. Maintenance teams also checked sensors and updated route information. The shuttle reduced certain repetitive driving tasks, but it created new work in supervision and system support. The university also had to decide how passengers would request help if the vehicle stopped unexpectedly. Designers added an accessible communication system and a clear procedure for emergency response. The project team tracked not only travel time but also interruptions and the time required for staff to resolve them. These measurements made the hidden support work visible. A passenger might see an empty driver's seat, yet several people still contributed to making the service dependable. The project showed that automation often changes the distribution of human responsibility rather than making it disappear. Understanding the real impact of an autonomous technology therefore requires examining the entire operating system, not only the machine performing the visible task.

readings.title: Food That Arrived Too Late
readings.passageEn: A city ran a program to move unsold food from shops to community centers. Organizers initially measured success by the total weight of collected food. Their monthly report looked impressive, but several centers said that deliveries sometimes arrived too late to distribute fresh items safely. Volunteers also spent long hours sorting products that were not suitable for local needs. The team added new measures: the share of food used, delivery time, and the resources required to handle each collection. With these numbers, coordinators changed collection routes and requested better information from participating shops. The case showed that a large output figure can hide weak results if the system's actual purpose is not considered. The coordinators learned that a shop could report a large quantity of surplus food without specifying how long it would remain usable. Collection teams sometimes arrived with vehicles that were too small for the available products or too large for a single stop. Better information about quantity, time, and handling requirements changed the route-planning problem. The objective was no longer to collect the largest possible weight at any cost; it was to deliver usable food with limited volunteer time. Meaningful performance measures should reflect whether useful food reaches people in good condition.

readings.title: The Essay Written with AI
readings.passageEn: A student used a writing assistant to suggest a first draft of an English essay. The sentences sounded fluent, but one paragraph referred to an experiment that the student could not find in the assigned article. At first, she wanted to submit the draft because it looked professional. Her teacher asked her to compare each factual claim with the source and rewrite the argument in her own words. She removed the unsupported example, kept some useful structure, and added an explanation she could defend. The experience showed that fluent language and reliable reasoning are not the same thing. The teacher explained that a convincing academic paragraph must connect its claim, evidence, and reasoning. A polished sentence can hide a missing link just as easily as a badly written one. The student began using the assistant to suggest questions she should ask of her draft rather than to provide a finished answer. This made the tool part of a checking process. It also gave her a clearer sense of which ideas she understood well enough to explain herself. AI assistance can save effort, but the learner remains responsible for checking evidence, understanding the content, and deciding what to say.

readings.title: Paying for Solar Panels
readings.passageEn: A small school considered installing solar panels on its roof. Supporters pointed to lower electricity costs over many years. Others worried that the initial purchase would use money needed for classroom repairs. The school prepared several scenarios for future electricity prices, maintenance expenses, and the panels' useful life. It also considered whether to install the whole system immediately or begin with a smaller section. The team learned that the cheapest choice today was not necessarily the least expensive over ten years, but the largest investment was not automatically best either. The finance committee distinguished initial spending from costs that would arise later, such as repairs and replacement components. It also considered whether electricity savings would remain valuable if prices fell rather than rose. Because the school could not predict every future condition, it did not rely on a single best-case forecast. The smaller initial installation had an advantage: it left money available for urgent classroom needs while creating an opportunity to learn from actual performance. A sensible long-term plan must compare uncertain future benefits with immediate limits on money and other resources.

readings.title: Does the Phone Cause Poor Sleep?
readings.passageEn: A student survey found that classmates who used their phones late at night often reported sleeping fewer hours. Some students immediately concluded that late phone use caused all sleep problems. Their teacher asked what else might explain the pattern. Students with heavy homework could stay awake longer and use their phones during breaks. Anxiety about an upcoming test might also affect both behavior and sleep. The survey identified a relationship, but it could not by itself separate these explanations. The class discussed how a controlled study or additional observations might help. Students proposed gathering more detailed information about bedtime routines and workload, although they knew that asking classmates about personal habits required care. They discussed the difference between observing a pattern and actively changing one factor in a well-designed study. The teacher stressed that even a controlled experiment would need to consider fairness and consent. A plausible explanation is a starting point for investigation, not a replacement for it. Evidence of association can guide good questions, but it should not be treated as proof of a single cause without further investigation.

readings.title: A Town Ready for Disruption
readings.passageEn: A coastal town depended on one road connecting its market to nearby farms. During a severe storm, the road closed and fresh food deliveries stopped. Afterward, officials considered building a second route. Farmers suggested adding small storage facilities as well, so essential goods would be available for a limited time even if transport failed. The town compared the cost of extra roads and storage with the disruption each option could absorb. Maintaining backup capacity seemed wasteful on normal days, when the original road worked well. The council also considered cooperation with nearby towns. If the road closed again, a temporary agreement might allow food to arrive through another market. However, that route could also fail during a regional storm. The planners therefore compared risks that affected only one road with risks that could affect several routes at once. They were willing to spend some resources on options that might rarely be used, provided the protection justified the cost. Yet the storm had shown that efficiency during ordinary conditions is not the same as resilience under pressure. The town's task was to choose a reasonable level of protection without assuming that every future emergency could be prevented.

readings.title: When One Rule Fits Nobody
readings.passageEn: A school introduced the same daily reading target for every student. The rule was easy to explain, but teachers soon noticed problems. Confident readers finished quickly and became bored, while beginners struggled to understand short texts under the time limit. The school changed the program so that all students still practiced regularly but worked with different levels of difficulty. Teachers monitored both comprehension and participation, then adjusted targets as students improved. The revised program was harder to manage because it required more information and judgment. Nevertheless, it better matched the goal of helping each learner make progress. The school also avoided labeling students permanently as strong or weak readers. Teachers reassessed their needs regularly and allowed movement between levels. A student who struggled with science articles might understand historical stories very well, showing that ability could depend partly on the topic. The new system made space for both challenge and support. Flexibility required careful observation instead of simply lowering expectations for some students. A rule can be simple and consistent without being suitable for every person or situation.

readings.title: A More Equitable Bus Plan
readings.passageEn: A city evaluated a proposed change to its local bus network. The plan would make popular routes more frequent, improving average waiting time across the city. Yet several neighborhoods with few passengers would lose their only direct connection to a hospital. At a public meeting, planners explained that maximizing the average benefit might overlook residents with limited travel choices. They compared alternative plans using both total passenger time and access to essential services. The final proposal kept some low-demand routes while improving busy corridors. It did not maximize a single numerical measure, but it served a broader public purpose. The planners noticed that the people most affected by a lost route were not always the people who attended public meetings. They consulted health centers and community organizations to learn how residents traveled for essential appointments. Some riders could transfer to another bus, but others faced long walks or additional fares. The city therefore examined the distribution of travel burdens rather than relying on one citywide average to summarize all experiences. Fairness in transport planning requires attention to the people behind the averages, especially those who have fewer alternatives.

readings.title: The Last Quiz
readings.passageEn: At the end of a twelve-week English project, a student compared her first diagnostic test with a new assessment. Her vocabulary score had improved, but she still made mistakes when reading passages about unfamiliar topics. She was tempted to memorize more word lists and avoid difficult texts. Her teacher suggested a different response: keep a short record of what each mistake revealed. Some errors came from unknown vocabulary, while others came from missing a contrast or assuming a detail was the main idea. The student planned new practice sessions for each weakness. The final assessment was not a judgment that her learning was finished. It was a tool for deciding what to work on next. During the project, the student had learned that the same wrong answer could result from different causes. A mistake made while guessing after a rushed reading session did not require the same response as a missing grammar concept. Her new notebook separated errors by type and noted a small action for the next session. She could now explain her own improvement more clearly than by reporting a single test score. The process made learning feel like a series of questions she could investigate. Learning becomes more sustainable when evaluation leads to a specific new question rather than a permanent label.

passages.title: A Different Way to Remember
passages.passageEn: Doyun studied a list of twenty words by reading each word and its meaning ten times. He felt confident when the words looked familiar. The next day, however, he could not remember several meanings without seeing his notes. His friend suggested covering the meanings and trying to recall them before checking the answers. The method felt harder, but it showed exactly which words needed more practice. Doyun also reviewed these words again a few days later. He noticed that feeling familiar with an answer was not always the same as being able to produce it. A small test without hints can reveal the difference between recognition and memory.

passages.title: A Window for Everyone
passages.passageEn: A community center planned to replace old windows to reduce heating costs. The manager chose a design that looked most efficient on paper. During a meeting, however, several visitors pointed out that the new windows were difficult to open for people with limited hand strength. The center compared other designs and found one that saved slightly less energy but was easier for more visitors to use. The staff did not ignore efficiency. They reconsidered how it should be measured alongside accessibility. A solution that performs well on one technical measure may still fail to serve the people for whom it was built.

passages.title: A Number Without a Story
passages.passageEn: An online report announced that a school's reading score had risen by fifteen points. The headline sounded impressive. A student asked whether the test had changed, how many pupils had taken it, and what the original score had been. The report did not provide those details. Her teacher explained that a number can describe a real change while still leaving important questions unanswered. The class searched for the full report and discovered that the school had introduced a different test. They could not directly compare the two scores without more information. Numerical evidence becomes meaningful only when readers understand how it was produced and what it can legitimately support.

passages.title: The Efficient but Fragile System
passages.passageEn: A town connected all neighborhood stores to one central warehouse. On ordinary days, the arrangement lowered transport costs because trucks could carry fuller loads. The town council proudly reported the savings. Then a road closure prevented vehicles from reaching the warehouse for two days. Stores on that side of town quickly ran short of certain products, even though supplies existed elsewhere. The council realized that it had measured efficiency under typical conditions but not the consequences of a rare disruption. Members explored backup routes and smaller storage points. These options would increase costs in ordinary weeks, yet they might protect essential deliveries during emergencies. Evaluating a system requires attention to both daily performance and its ability to absorb unexpected failures.
